anchors.paper_title: Probability estimation of narcolepsy type 1 in DTA mice using unlabeled EEG and EMG data
anchors.reason: Paper builds an NT1 phenotype pipeline in DTA mice, trained partly on 83 WT mice; the dataset has only healthy mice and the paper doesn't clearly introduce it, despite author overlap.

metadata.methods_description: Recordings from 92 healthy mice across five labs each include at least one EEG and one EMG channel, with the number of EEG channels varying by lab. Each mouse was scored by a single sleep expert using 4-second epochs. All recordings were downsampled to 128 Hz, expressed in volts, and stored in EDF format.

citation_details.title: Cross-Band Coupling of EEG Infraslow Oscillations during NREM Sleep in Mice
citation_details.author: Max Tan, Oscar D. Ramírez‐Plascencia, Wei Wang, Amanda Studnicki, J. Kent Werner, Elizaveta A. Tremsina, Shiqian Shen, Can Zhang, Tingying Helen Zeng, ROBERT JOSEPH THOMAS, Haoqi Sun
citation_details.abstract: Abstract The infraslow oscillation (ISO) is a ~ 0.02 Hz rhythmic fluctuation in electroencephalographic (EEG) power during NREM sleep. Prior studies were limited to sigma-band ISO, linked to rhythmic norepinephrine release in mice. Whether ISOs exist in other bands, and how ISOs across bands are coupled, remain unknown. We analyzed cross-band ISO coupling across six frequency bands during NREM using a wild-type (WT) discovery dataset of 122 recordings from 72 mice and WT validation of 7 mice. A transgenic (TG) validation of 6 mice was added to test ISO coupling’s robustness to Cre knock-in on the LepR gene (LepR-Cre). Band power time series were filtered to the ISO range of 0.01–0.03 Hz. Cross-band coupling was assessed using Spearman’s correlation and phase-locking value (PLV) across all 15 band pairs. ISOs were strongest in alpha, sigma, beta, and theta bands, weak in gamma, and absent in delta. Alpha, sigma, beta, and theta ISOs formed a highly correlated motif with replication in WT and TG (r = 0.61–0.77), while gamma had moderate correlation (r = 0.30–0.42), and delta was uncorrelated (p > 0.05). All band pairs showed significant phase locking with replication (FDR-corrected q < 0.01), with stronger consistency in alpha, sigma, theta, and beta (PLV 0.54–0.71), and weaker consistency involving delta and gamma (PLV 0.12–0.37). EEG ISOs extend beyond the sigma band to alpha, beta, and theta bands, forming a strongly coupled motif that may reflect a fundamental organization principle of sleep microstructures at a minute scale.

citation_details.title: Somnus, a tunable, open-source platform for automated EEG sleep scoring in physiological and disease mouse models
citation_details.author: Joshua M. Brenner, Matthew S. Caudill, Huda Yahya Zoghbi
citation_details.abstract: Many studies using mouse models of human brain disorders rely on extended recordings of brain electrical activity through electroencephalogram, or EEG. The features that researchers measure in these recordings, such as seizures and epileptiform activity, are deeply influenced by whether the animal is awake, in non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, or in rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. Because total sleep duration varies naturally across animals, rigorous experimental comparisons require classifying the sleep state of every few seconds of a recording. Manual annotation is highly labor-intensive, often requiring hours per subject. While automated scoring tools accelerate this process, they are typically trained exclusively on healthy cohorts and frequently fail when applied to disease models that exhibit atypical or fragmented sleep architecture. Somnus is an open-source Python package designed to automate rodent sleep staging using EEG, muscle activity (EMG), and optional video-tracking data. It includes a robust base model trained on diverse recordings from six independent laboratories, enabling out-of-the-box classification across various equipment setups without requiring prior manual labeling. A central feature of Somnus is its capacity for rapid adaptation to pathological sleep structure. The software provides a graphical interface that directs researchers to the specific epochs where the base model is least certain. Users can manually correct these targeted epochs in a built-in viewer by comparing the model's classification to the raw EEG signal and video, and then use their corrections to fine-tune the model. This workflow empowers researchers to generate accurate custom scorers for complex disease models or novel treatments with just a few minutes of manual correction, bypassing the need to hand-score entire experimental cohorts or develop their own models from scratch.
